cf.title: Check the fd number against FD_SETSIZE in PQsocketPoll

input.subject: Check the fd number against FD_SETSIZE in PQsocketPoll

verdict_reasoning: One objection survived, maintenance-fit-1, and it is a fixable level 2 point about where the fix belongs. The guard itself replaces an out-of-bounds FD_SET() with an EINVAL failure and nobody objected to that. A committer who knows the libpq portability code has to decide between guarding the non-Windows select() fallback and removing it. Confidence is low because the thread has only the author's two messages and names no platform that compiles the branch.

brief.title: libpq: check socket fd against FD_SETSIZE in PQsocketPoll select fallback
brief.problem: On platforms without poll(2), PQsocketPoll() falls back to select(2) and calls FD_SET() on the connection socket without checking its number. If the socket fd is at or above FD_SETSIZE, FD_SET() writes past the fd_set on the stack. This affects libpq client applications that hold many open files before connecting.
brief.proposed_design: In the select() fallback, PQsocketPoll() checks the socket fd against FD_SETSIZE and fails with EINVAL instead of calling FD_SET(). v2 skips the check on Windows, where fd_set is a bounded array and FD_SET() checks its limits. The change is in src/interfaces/libpq/fe-misc.c only.
user_visible_surface: PQsocketPoll() can now fail with EINVAL when the socket fd is at or above FD_SETSIZE, on non-Windows platforms without poll(2).
author_claims: The unchecked FD_SET() in the select() fallback can corrupt the stack.
The fix is cheap and worth having as a defence.
The issue is mostly theoretical, since modern systems have poll(2) and do not compile this branch.
Testing on Windows showed the check is not needed there.
brief.thread_state: Only the author has posted: the first message with v1 and a follow-up with v2 that drops Windows. No reviewer has replied.
unclear: The patch does not name any supported platform that lacks poll(2) and so would compile this branch.
The proposal does not say how PQsocketPoll() reports EINVAL to callers, or whether its documentation changes.
The proposal does not say whether other select() call sites in libpq or the client tools need the same check.
The material shows no test that covers the new error path.

objections.title: Guard goes into a branch no supported Unix may compile
objections.failure_scenario: v2 adds a new error path to the non-Windows select() fallback in PQsocketPoll(). If no buildfarm animal builds that branch, a later change to fe-misc.c can break it with no one noticing. The first report then comes from a user on a rare platform, and no committer can reproduce it.
objections.argument: Message #2 says the remaining case is "mostly theoretical", and the proposal names no supported platform that lacks poll(2). Code that is never compiled or run in testing costs review time now and can rot later. A committer would likely ask whether the right change is to require poll(2) on non-Windows platforms and drop that branch, which removes the risk instead of guarding it. The guard is small, so this is about where the fix goes.
objections.author_must_show: Which supported platform or buildfarm animal compiles the non-Windows select() fallback today, and if none does, why keep and extend that branch instead of removing it?

critic.reasoning: Message #2 calls the remaining case "mostly theoretical", and the material names no supported non-Windows platform without poll(2). Windows builds compile the select() branch, but v2 skips the guard there, so nothing builds or tests the new check.

refuted.title: No supported platform named that compiles the guarded branch
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer adds an EINVAL path to a select() branch that no buildfarm animal compiles. No user ever reaches it, and a later edit to PQsocketPoll() can break it without any test or build failing. Nobody notices until someone ports libpq to a system without poll(2).
refuted.argument: The author calls the remaining case "mostly theoretical" in message #2, after Windows was dropped. The material names no supported Unix without poll(2), and no user report of the failure. The benefit is a defence for a platform that may not exist among supported targets, while the untested branch stays in the tree. A committer would likely ask for a named platform, or would prefer removing the select() fallback on non-Windows builds to guarding it.
refuted.author_must_show: Which currently supported, non-Windows platform builds libpq without poll(2), so that this branch is compiled and tested?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which makes the same point about the untested branch and also states the alternative of requiring poll(2) on non-Windows builds.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: PQsocketPoll() is a public libpq function and gains a new EINVAL failure case; its signature does not change.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The patch replaces an out-of-bounds stack write in the client-side select() fallback with an error return.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The CommitFest entry is tagged Bugfix, so a committer has to decide whether to backpatch the guard.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The new error path sits in a select() branch that, per message #2, no known non-Windows platform compiles.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which supported platform or buildfarm animal compiles the non-Windows select() fallback in PQsocketPoll() today?
If no supported platform compiles that branch, why guard it instead of requiring poll(2) on non-Windows builds and removing it?
Do other select() call sites in libpq or the client tools call FD_SET() on an unchecked fd and need the same check?
Is the guard meant for backpatching, as the Bugfix tag suggests, or for master only?
How can the new EINVAL path be tested if no buildfarm animal builds the branch?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows libpq's socket code and the platform portability rules (which systems must have poll(2)) would have to own it. No reviewer has replied in the thread.
committability.liability: A new error path in a branch that may never be compiled or tested, for as long as the select() fallback stays in the tree. The size is small: one check in one file.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v2 the same day after testing on Windows, which suggests responsiveness. The thread is two weeks old and has no reviewer feedback to respond to yet.

priority.reason: The patch is about 1.4 KB in one file, and message #2 calls the remaining case "mostly theoretical". The open point is whether to guard the non-Windows select() fallback or remove it, and that should be settled before code review.

provisional_note: The code was not read. I could not check how the guard is placed relative to FD_SET(), how v2 excludes Windows, or whether other select() call sites have the same gap.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Enable parallel SELECT for "INSERT INTO ... SELECT ..."."
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Enable parallel SELECT for "INSERT INTO ... SELECT ..."."
Reverted commit(s): Doc: Update description for parallel insert reloption.; Add a new GUC and a reloption to enable inserts in parallel-mode.; Improve FK trigger parallel-safety check added by 05c8482f7f.; Enable parallel SELECT for "INSERT INTO ... SELECT ...".; Fix use of relcache TriggerDesc field introduced by commit 05c8482f7f.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
To allow inserts in parallel-mode this feature has to ensure that all the
constraints, triggers, etc. are parallel-safe for the partition hierarchy
which is costly and we need to find a better way to do that. Additionally,
we could have used existing cached information in some cases like indexes,
domains, etc. to determine the parallel-safety.

List of commits reverted, in reverse chronological order:

ed62d3737c Doc: Update description for parallel insert reloption.
c8f78b6161 Add a new GUC and a reloption to enable inserts in parallel-mode.
c5be48f092 Improve FK trigger parallel-safety check added by 05c8482f7f.
e2cda3c20a Fix use of relcache TriggerDesc field introduced by commit 05c8482f7f.
e4e87a32cc Fix valgrind issue in commit 05c8482f7f.
05c8482f7f Enable parallel SELECT for "INSERT INTO ... SELECT ...".

precedents_retrieved.title: Parallel INSERT (INTO ... SELECT ...)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set allows parallel execution of both the INSERT and the SELECT parts of "INSERT INTO ... SELECT ...", with workers inserting tuples themselves; where parallel insert is unsafe (for example foreign keys or ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE), only the SELECT part is parallelised. It changes the planner, executor and parallel-worker code, adds parallel-safety checks on the target table (including partitions, triggers and domains), and adds a GUC and a reloption to control the feature.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Parts of the work, "Parallel SELECT for INSERT" and the related GUC/reloption, were committed during the thread. The remaining patches, which add the parallel INSERT functionality itself, were marked Returned with Feedback because of feedback given on pgsql-committers, which said a lot of work remained. The visible messages do not show the content of that feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There is a lot of work
to do for this patch as per the feedback given on pgsql-committers
[1].

precedents_retrieved.title: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT [FOR ...]
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds ON CONFLICT DO SELECT to INSERT, which returns the conflicting row through RETURNING instead of updating it, with an optional row lock (DO SELECT FOR UPDATE and similar). It revives a 2017 patch by Marko and rebases it for table AMs, EXPLAIN, RLS and OLD/NEW in RETURNING.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Dean Rasheed found the patch not yet committable. Partitioned tables crashed with DO SELECT FOR UPDATE, the docs did not cover DO SELECT, and regression and isolation tests were missing. The author agreed and said a new version would follow, but none was posted before the entry was closed in August 2025.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think there is still a fair bit more to do to get this into a
committable state. The docs in particular need work.

precedents_retrieved.title: Relax requirement for INTO with SELECT in pl/pgsql
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets a pl/pgsql SELECT, or a DML statement with RETURNING, run without INTO and discard its result instead of raising "query has no destination for result data". This would deprecate PERFORM and bring pl/pgsql closer to plain SQL.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The idea had broad support (+1 from Jim, Merlin, Robert, Tom, David J. and Brendan Jurd). Pavel Stehule's -1 rested on the SQL standard and Oracle, both of which require INTO, but he later called his opinion minor. David G. Johnston's review asked for reworked documentation and at least one new test. Merlin Moncure agreed to resubmit but sent no updated patch, so Peter Eisentraut returned it with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think we are waiting on an updated patch, with docs and tests.

precedents_retrieved.title: Tab completion for SELECT in psql
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds psql tab completion after SELECT, suggesting column names from all visible tables and function names. Functions that are unlikely to be called directly are filtered out, and later versions use per-server-version queries and add completion after commas.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas found the completions both too broad and too narrow: system catalog columns flood short prefixes, the FROM clause is ignored, and system columns appear inconsistently. He held that the completion must be smarter to be acceptable. He also reported that the query on pg_attribute took about 1 second on a database with a 1000-partition table. An earlier review by Peter Eisentraut found broken older-version queries and an unsettled function filter. The rebased patch of 2018-09-22 got no visible reply before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think the completion needs to be smarter to be acceptable.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fallback table AM for relkinds without storage
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a fallback table AM whose callbacks all raise an error, and assign it to relkinds without storage (views, foreign tables, partitioned tables) so that rd_tableam is never NULL. A wrong call into the table AM API for such a relation would then raise an error instead of crashing the backend.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected that the patch moves relkind-specific logic, such as choosing the slot type, into an AM that should never be called. He suggested separate AMs instead, for example one for foreign tables and one for sequences. Michael Paquier agreed he was not comfortable passing relkind knowledge into the AM, and he returned the entry because he was not sure what the right design was.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This doesn't seem like an advantage to me. Isn't this just pushing logic
away from a fairly obvious point into an AM that one would expect to
never actually get called?

precedents_retrieved.title: Use AF_UNIX for tests on Windows (ie drop fallback TCP code)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Thomas Munro proposed using AF_UNIX sockets for pg_regress and TAP tests on Windows too, removing the Windows-only TCP and SSPI setup code in the test harness. To match Unix security, mkdtemp() on Windows would create the socket directory with access for the current user only.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that with TCP gone from the Windows tests, the TCP socket code would have little test coverage on any platform, and reviewers asked for a switch that runs the tests over either TCP or Unix sockets. The author agreed, set the TAP test patch aside for more work and posted only the first two patches. Those later stopped applying, the author posted no new version, and the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If we remove that, won't we have a whole lot of code that's not
tested at all on any platform, ie all the TCP-socket code?

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert misguided change to postgres_fdw FOR UPDATE/SHARE code.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert misguided change to postgres_fdw FOR UPDATE/SHARE code.
Reverted commit(s): Fix planning of SELECT FOR UPDATE on child table with partial index.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit 462bd95705a0c23ba0b0ba60a78d32566a0384c1, I changed postgres_fdw
to rely on get_plan_rowmark() instead of get_parse_rowmark().  I still
think that's a good idea in the long run, but as Etsuro Fujita pointed out,
it doesn't work today because planner.c forces PlanRowMarks to have
markType = ROW_MARK_COPY for all foreign tables.  There's no urgent reason
to change this in the back branches, so let's just revert that part of
yesterday's commit rather than trying to design a better solution under
time pressure.

Also, add a regression test case showing what postgres_fdw does with FOR
UPDATE/SHARE.  I'd blithely assumed there was one already, else I'd have
realized yesterday that this code didn't work.

precedents_retrieved.title: INSERT SELECT: BulkInsertState and table_multi_insert
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make INSERT, including INSERT SELECT and INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, use a BulkInsertState ring buffer as COPY does, so data loaders do not leave many dirty buffers in shared buffers. Later versions added a GUC to opt in, and switched to table_multi_insert after a set number of tuples.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread stalled. The multi-insert part became complex: it cannot handle volatile column defaults, and the author proposed leaving it to the separate "New Table Access Methods for Multi and Single Inserts" patch. The author split off the simple BulkInsertState patch and said to close the entry if no one was interested in it alone. No reviewer took that patch up, so the commitfest manager proposed closing it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Since the thread has stalled, maybe that's the best course of action here.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix out-of-bounds with function PQescapeInternal
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the buffer size that PQescapeInternal in libpq allocates on its slow path, adding two bytes per quote or backslash. It followed a Coverity report of an out-of-bounds write in pg_createsubscriber.c.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane replied that each quote or backslash is already counted in input_len, so one extra byte per character is enough. He added an Assert that the buffer is filled exactly, and check-world passed. The author checked with a debugger, found no overrun, called the Coverity warning wrong, and withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Nonsense.  The quote or backslash is already counted in input_len,
so we need to add just one more.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "libpqwalreceiver: Convert to libpq-be-fe-helpers.h"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "libpqwalreceiver: Convert to libpq-be-fe-helpers.h"
Reverted commit(s): libpqwalreceiver: Convert to libpq-be-fe-helpers.h
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 728f86fec65537eade8d9e751961782ddb527934.

The signal handling was a few bricks shy of a load in that commit,
which made the walreceiver non-responsive to SIGTERM while it was
waiting for the connection to be established. That prevented a standby
from being promoted.

Since it was non-essential refactoring, let's revert it to make v16
work the same as earlier releases. I reverted it in 'master' too, to
keep the branches in sync. The refactoring was a good idea as such,
but it needs a bit more work. Once we have developed a complete patch
with this issue fixed, let's re-apply that to 'master'.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P13] concerns pgbench connection limits on Windows, a different program, and records no reason, so nothing from it applies here. Message #1 points to a separate pgbench FD_SETSIZE thread as the starting point, and the material does not report how that thread ended.

From the standards and compatibility angle there is nothing to object to. PQsocketPoll() already returns -1 with errno set on failure, so EINVAL fits that contract and replaces undefined behaviour; no syntax, GUC, catalog, pg_dump or psql surface changes, and only builds without poll(2) are affected.

The patch changes only the select() fallback in libpq's fe-misc.c, so there is nothing for this angle to review. It touches no on-disk format, WAL, catalog, replication or wire protocol message, and PQsocketPoll() keeps its signature and its existing -1-with-errno failure convention, so ABI and backpatching are unaffected.

The patch adds no privilege, role, setting or exposure, and only replaces an out-of-bounds FD_SET() in the client-side select() fallback with an EINVAL failure. That makes the code safer, and the only fd numbers involved belong to the client process, so I see no security objection.

The only objection concerns where the fix belongs. The change is small, touches one file, and adds no cost on any hot path. [P13] has no recorded reason and covers pgbench on Windows, so I do not cite it.

No existing Postgres feature, setting or extension guards PQsocketPoll() against fds at or above FD_SETSIZE in its select() fallback, so this angle has nothing to raise. Whether the branch should be removed outright, given that the author calls it theoretical, belongs to the desirability and design angles.
One objection only. The change is small and a memory-safety guard, so the cost is low. The open point is whether any supported user can reach the guarded code.
